newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli archaeologists find ancient mass grave.
newsitem.headline: Israeli archaeologists find ancient mass grave.

text.p: Israeli archaeologists have discovered a mass grave in Galilee dating from an AD 67 Jewish revolt against Rome.
"We uncovered in a cistern many, many people, including young children and teen-agers about 16 years old," archaeologist Mordechai Aviam said on Tuesday.
"Those are probably families that died in the siege," he said.

Roman forces besieged the city of Yodfat in their march on Jerusalem and captured it after 47 days. The discovery confirms reports of Jewish historian Josephus, who survived the attack by surrendering to the Romans.
Josephus, also a military commander, described a bloody battle in which warriors from Yodfat frequently descended from the city to attack the Roman camp.

When the Romans finally broke into the city, Josephus and 40 other men hid in a cave. Refusing to surrender, they systematically killed one another until only Josephus and one other man were left alive.
After they surrendered, Josephus accompanied the Roman army in chains as it conquered all of ancient Israel, recording those events.
Aviam said Josephus' description leads him to believe the bones he found a week ago are of people who died in the siege.
"The Jews who came back buried them in a cistern," he said. "This is the first time we can identify the people who died."
Archaeologists also discovered the bones of a soldier on the frescoed floor of a Yodfat mansion.

The mansion, decorated in geometric patterns and "better than Masada" may contain the most well-preserved frescoes ever discovered in Israel. Masada is the hilltop site of a famous battle between Jews and Romans where other frescoes were found.
"This is the first place in Israel where we have a frescoed floor. It's something only rich people can do," Aviam said.
"You don't find it in Herodian palaces and you don't find it in Jerusalem."
Aviam, who is in the sixth and final season of excavations he is conducting with a University of Rochester professor, said he believed Yodfat was wealthier than Josephus indicated.
"They were not all poor. Now we have evidence of at least one very rich family," he said. "It was maybe a centre for culture...like Caesarea."
